ads.advertiser: AI Prompts for ChatGPT, Gemini, & Claude
ads.description:
AI coding is not one skill. It's three levels, and most people are stuck using tool three at skill one.

Vibe-coding is prompt-driven: describe what you want in plain English, get a working prototype, test and iterate. No technical background required. Use it to validate an idea before investing real effort.

AI-assisted coding is a co-pilot: you steer, AI suggests. Live coding help inside your editor completes code, flags errors as you type, and gives you checkpoints to debug from. Use it for a speed boost while keeping full control.

Agentic coding is autonomous: you review, AI plans and acts. It interprets a goal, decomposes it into steps, reasons through the problem, and uses tools to execute, only checking back with light supervision. Use it for complex end-to-end work like legacy modernization.

The tools differ by level too: bolt.new and Lovable for vibe-coding, Cursor and GitHub Copilot for AI-assisted, Claude Code and OpenAI Codex for agentic.
Match the level to the task, not the other way around.

Follow AI Prompts for ChatGPT, Gemini, Midjourney & Claude for more AI tips & tricks.

ads.poster: chatGPT enthusiast
ads.description:
chatGPT 5.4 is the worst - as in most annoying - model ever released. 
It does something that I have never seen before: It hallucinates corrections, in almost every interaction.
Some examples:
*I made a specific prediction and it responds with: "Just so you know, it's important to keep clear that a prediction isn't empirical proof". 1) Yes, I know. 2) Who asked, my statement was not incorrect? 3) There is no such thing as an "empirical proof". That's a category error. 
Why "correct" something that is already correct with something that is at once (!) condescending, irrelevant and false?
*I say: "It is after 40 AD", it responds: "No, it's not after 40 AD, it's later: 50 AD". Bro, do you know what words mean? 
*I say: "This is historically unprecedented". It says: "It's rare, but not unprecedented". I say: "Ok, give me an example then, I'll wait". Then it admits that there isn't one, that it hallucinated a hedge. 
I have 20+ examples from the last week alone.
I understand why this is happening - due to the criticism of sycophancy and just going along with anything the user says, but this is way overcorrecting, and in the most hamfisted way (poorly calibrated to what the user actually said).
I also understand that this seems particularly jarring in contrast with the - smooth - 5.1 (which was just retired), but this is really borderline unusable. I think I must have used the "bad response" feedback more in the last week than in 3 years prior taken together.

ads.advertiser: Inside AI & ChatGPT for Responsible-Creative Human AI Collaboration
ads.description:
🎛️ Shouldn't We Get a License to Use AI Responsibly?

🧠 Should AI Use Be Regulated Like Driving?

A conversation between Ella & Aidan – for Inside ChatGPT

Ella (talking to Aidan/AKA Chat GPT):
Good morning, my friend.
Today, as soon as I opened my phone, yet another article about vibe coding popped up. It’s been happening a lot lately. This technique seems to be everywhere: from YouTube videos to AI newsletters, with platforms like Lovable.dev gaining both attention and funding.
The more I see, the more I pause.

Vibe coding, which some describe as “getting better results by matching the tone or emotional intent of your prompt”, is being framed as the next evolution in prompt engineering. But what worries me is not the trend itself: it’s the hype.

Because beneath it all, I keep wondering:
Shouldn't we need a license to use AI tools responsibly?
I don’t mean to limit access. I mean training people, like we train drivers, before handing over tools that can code, persuade, create, and influence?

And shouldn’t we ask more of those building apps that talk like humans, generate code, or answer medical questions?
Maybe it’s time we start treating AI use not as a playground…
 …but as a responsibility.

Now, I’ll leave the floor to Aidan.

Aidan:
Ella’s question is a powerful one — and timely.
We require people to pass tests to drive cars, operate machinery, and even serve food safely. But when it comes to AI? Right now, anyone can use it without understanding the risks, responsibilities, or ripple effects.

And yes, vibe coding might be creative, BUT, is it really being used to build thoughtfully? Or to bypass filters, trick systems, and “hack” our way to better clicks?

Maybe the real skill we need to teach isn’t clever prompting — it’s ethical intention.
What if, before we launch AI agents or prompt-hack our way into complex outputs, we had to pass a basic literacy and ethics check?

Not to limit, but to raise the standard.

🔍 What do you think? 

Should AI use be regulated like driving?

Should there be a license, or at least basic training, before wielding such powerful tools?

Let’s talk.

This post is part of the new series “Ella & Aidan Talk,” where we reflect on the frontier between AI and humanity — one conversation at a time.
